stories.title: A journey from war to hope
stories.content:
With the outbreak of the Syrian civil war in 2011, millions of Syrians were forced to leave their country in search of safety, fleeing violence and insecurity.
Cyprus was one of the closest European destinations reached by refugees, with some crossing the sea in difficult and dangerous journeys.
In Nicosia and other cities, Syrian families began new lives from scratch. They faced challenges with language, work, and integration, yet showed great strength in adapting and moving forward.
Children enrolled in schools and learned a new language, while adults worked in various fields to build a better future for their families.
Despite all the hardships, memories remain vivid, and the hope of returning home one day never leaves them.
This story represents thousands of similar stories—carrying pain within them, but also filled with hope and determination.

stories.title: A Refuge Remembered: The Armenians of Nicosia
stories.content:
Cyprus has been home to an Armenian community for over a thousand years, but its modern story is one of survival. In the years after 1915, thousands of Armenians fleeing the genocide in the Ottoman Empire found refuge on the island, and Nicosia became a heart of their new life.

In 1926, the Melkonian Educational Institute opened its doors on the edge of the city. Founded by two brothers to care for orphans of the genocide, it grew into one of the most important Armenian schools in the world, a place where children from across the diaspora came to learn their language, music, and history, and to keep an identity alive that others had tried to erase.

For generations, the Armenian quarter of old Nicosia echoed with Western Armenian, in its church, its school, and its family bakeries. Like other communities on the island, the Armenians were displaced and divided by the events of 1974, yet they remained one of Cyprus's officially recognised communities, woven into the fabric of the country.

This pin marks a place of memory and resilience. It is where a community that lost almost everything rebuilt itself, and where the Armenian language and spirit still endure in the streets, churches, and stories of Nicosia.

stories.title: A Palestinian Engineer Building a Life in Cyprus
stories.content:
Wasif Almady is a stateless Palestinian who came to Cyprus in 2010 after living in Iraq. He and his family fled the violence and persecution that followed the Iraq War. In Cyprus, Wasif continued his education and worked in different roles, including teaching at an Arabic-speaking private school in Nicosia.

He later began PhD studies and worked on software projects for scientists and engineers. He also became a translator at the Kofinou Reception Center, where he encountered other refugees and heard their stories.

For Wasif, Cyprus became a place where he could build a safer life with his wife, children and mother. At the same time, his statelessness remained an important part of his identity. He described the experience of Palestinians as generations living without citizenship and a permanent sense of belonging.

His story represents more than migration: it shows how Palestinian refugees in Cyprus have built careers, families and communities while carrying memories of displacement and the continuing question of belonging.

stories.title: Nine Thousand Years of Memory: The Neolithic Village of Choirokoitia
stories.content:
Long before Cyprus had cities, palaces, or written history, people were already building round stone houses on a hillside above the Maroni river. Choirokoitia was settled almost nine thousand years ago, during the Neolithic period, making it one of the best-preserved prehistoric sites anywhere in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The people who lived here built circular dwellings from stone and mudbrick, thatched with branches and clay. They kept sheep and goats, ground grain by hand, and buried their dead beneath the floors of their own homes, a quiet way of keeping family close even in death.

In 1998, Choirokoitia was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised as one of the most important sources of knowledge about how human communities first organised themselves into permanent settlements in this part of the world.

This pin marks a place where the story of Cyprus does not begin with any single community, but with the very first people who chose this island as home. Every culture that came after, every wave of migration this map records, has its roots in that first decision to stay.

stories.title: Sanna: The Last Voices of Cypriot Maronite Arabic
stories.content:
In the village of Kormakitis and a handful of other communities, elderly Maronites still speak a language found nowhere else on earth: Sanna, or Cypriot Maronite Arabic. It arrived with Maronite refugees fleeing religious persecution in the Levant centuries ago, and over hundreds of years living alongside Greek Cypriots, it absorbed Greek grammar and vocabulary into its Arabic roots, becoming something entirely its own.

Sanna was never really a written language. It lived, and still lives, in the voice: in songs sung at family gatherings, in the words grandparents used for things their grandchildren now only know in Greek or English. Linguists classify it as severely endangered, with only around a thousand speakers left and almost no fluent speakers under the age of thirty.

In recent years, community members, linguists and the Maronite Church have worked together on documentation and revival projects, recording elders while their voices can still be heard, and trying to pass fragments of Sanna back to a younger generation.

This pin is a reminder that not every story is written down. Some live only in speech, passed voice to voice, and disappear the moment no one is left to listen. Sanna is still being spoken here, for now.

stories.title: Threads of Lefkara: A Village Stitched in Lace
stories.content:
In the hill village of Pano Lefkara, the sound of a Cypriot afternoon has, for centuries, included the quiet click of needles. Lefkaritika, or Lefkara lace, is said to date back to at least the fourteenth century, shaped by local needlework traditions and by the embroidery of Venetian nobility who once ruled the island.

The craft combines four techniques: hemstitching, cutwork, satin-stitch fillings and needlepoint edging, worked entirely by hand into tablecloths, veils and fine linens. It was never a solitary craft. Women gathered in the narrow streets and on shaded patios to work together, turning the making of lace into an ongoing, shared conversation passed from mother to daughter.

In 2009, UNESCO inscribed Lefkara lace on its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage, recognising not just the craft itself but the social life woven around it.

This pin marks a village where a needle and thread became a way for generations of women to keep talking to each other, and where that conversation, stitch by stitch, is still being had today.

stories.title: From Milk to Memory: The Story of Halloumi
stories.content:
In the villages of the Troodos foothills, cheese-making was never just a way to preserve milk through the seasons. It was a rhythm of rural life, passed down through families who kept sheep and goats on the same hillsides for generations. Their cheese, folded and salted in a way that lets it be grilled or fried without melting, became known across the island simply as halloumi.

In 2021, the European Union registered halloumi as a Protected Designation of Origin, meaning only cheese made in Cyprus to the traditional recipe may carry the name. Producers on both sides of the island were included in the protection, a rare piece of shared heritage recognised across every community.

For families in these hill villages, the cheese was never about branding. It was about a specific pot, a specific hillside, and the particular taste of milk from animals that grazed on wild thyme and oregano.

This pin marks the everyday side of cultural memory: the kind that is not found in a museum, but on a kitchen table, still being made the same way it always was.

stories.title: Tsiattista: When Two Communities Sing the Same Verse
stories.content:
On summer evenings in Cypriot villages, two singers would once stand across from each other, often accompanied by violin or lute, and begin to duel, not with instruments but with words. Tsiattista is a form of improvised sung poetry, built from rhyming couplets invented on the spot, each singer trying to outwit the other with wit, wordplay and sharp observation.

The tradition is not confined to one community. Tsiattista has long been practised by both Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot singers, sharing the same rhythms and rules across a divide that separates almost everything else on the island.

In 2011, UNESCO added tsiattista poetic duelling to its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage, recognising it as a living tradition still performed at weddings, festivals and village gatherings today.

This pin marks a form of storytelling that has always belonged to everyone on the island at once: proof that some traditions were shared long before anyone thought to divide them.

stories.title: Fifty Nations, One Cross: The Latins of Nicosia
stories.content:
In the old city of Nicosia stands the Church of the Holy Cross, home to one of Cyprus's smallest but oldest recognised communities: the Latins. Descendants of Catholic families with centuries of presence on the island, the Latin community was formally recognised as one of Cyprus's three religious minorities in the 1960 constitution, alongside the Maronites and Armenians.

The first church on this site was built in 1642. The current building, completed in 1902, was funded in part by the Spanish royal family and by Franciscan friars connected to the Holy Land, a small building carrying a very international history.

Today, Mass at Holy Cross is celebrated in as many as eight languages, reflecting a congregation that draws people from dozens of countries who have made Cyprus their home, alongside the descendants of the island's original Latin families.

This pin marks a community defined less by size than by continuity: a small congregation that has kept its place in Cyprus's story for hundreds of years, and continues to welcome new arrivals into it.

stories.title: Stone Tombs of Kings Who Were Never Kings
stories.content:
On the coast near Paphos lies an underground necropolis known, somewhat mysteriously, as the Tombs of the Kings. No king was ever buried here. The name comes from the extraordinary scale of the tombs, carved directly into solid rock and modelled on the houses of the living, which led locals long ago to assume only royalty could have afforded them.

In reality, the tombs belonged to Paphos's aristocracy and high officials during the Hellenistic and Roman periods, from around the third century BC onward. Some are decorated with Doric columns cut straight from the bedrock, surrounding open courtyards open to the sky, an architectural style found almost nowhere else in Cyprus.

The site forms part of the wider Paphos Archaeological Park, itself inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its exceptional concentration of ancient mosaics and monuments.

This pin marks a landmark built on a misunderstanding that has lasted over a century, a reminder that the stories a place accumulates can become as much a part of its heritage as the history that actually happened there.

stories.title: Skate day 2026
stories.content: Thank you all for coming down to celebrate Go Skate Day with us. People came through from different cities, different crews, different ages, all for the same thing: skateboarding. The energy was unreal from start to finish. Skaters, filmers, photographers, friends, shops, brands, and people passing by all added something to the day.

story_translations.title: Ένα Καταφύγιο που Μνημονεύεται: Οι Αρμένιοι της Λευκωσίας
story_translations.content: Η Κύπρος φιλοξενεί μια αρμενική κοινότητα για πάνω από χίλια χρόνια, αλλά η σύγχρονη ιστορία της είναι μια ιστορία επιβίωσης. Στα χρόνια μετά το 1915, χιλιάδες Αρμένιοι που διέφυγαν από τη γενοκτονία στην Οθωμανική Αυτοκρατορία βρήκαν καταφύγιο στο νησί, και η Λευκωσία έγινε η καρδιά της νέας τους ζωής. Το 1926, το Μελκονιανό Εκπαιδευτικό Ίδρυμα άνοιξε τις πύλες του στην άκρη της πόλης. Ιδρυμένο από δύο αδερφούς για να φροντίσει τα ορφανά της γενοκτονίας, εξελίχθηκε σε ένα από τα σπουδαιότερα αρμενικά σχολεία στον κόσμο, ένα μέρος όπου παιδιά από όλη τη διασπορά ήρθαν για να μάθουν τη γλώσσα, τη μουσική και την ιστορία τους, και να κρατήσουν ζωντανή μια ταυτότητα που άλλοι είχαν προσπαθήσει να σβήσουν. Για γενιές, η αρμενική συνοικία της παλιάς Λευκωσίας αντηχούσε στα δυτικά αρμενικά, στην εκκλησία της, στο σχολείο της και στους οικογενειακούς της φούρνους. Όπως και άλλες κοινότητες του νησιού, οι Αρμένιοι εκτοπίστηκαν και χωρίστηκαν από τα γεγονότα του 1974, ωστόσο παρέμειναν μία από τις επίσημα αναγνωρισμένες κοινότητες της Κύπρου, υφασμένοι στον ιστό της χώρας. Αυτή η πινέζα σηματοδοτεί έναν τόπο μνήμης και ανθεκτικότητας. Είναι το μέρος όπου μια κοινότητα που έχασε σχεδόν τα πάντα ανασυγκροτήθηκε, και όπου η αρμενική γλώσσα και το πνεύμα εξακολουθούν να αντέχουν στους δρόμους, τις εκκλησίες και τις ιστορίες της Λευκωσίας.

story_translations.title: Hatırlanan Bir Sığınak: Lefkoşa Ermenileri
story_translations.content:
Kıbrıs, bin yılı aşkın bir süredir bir Ermeni toplumuna ev sahipliği yapmaktadır, ancak buradaki modern hikâye bir hayatta kalma mücadelesidir. 1915'ten sonraki yıllarda, Osmanlı İmparatorluğu'ndaki soykırımdan kaçan binlerce Ermeni adada sığınak buldu ve Lefkoşa, yeni yaşamlarının merkezi hâline geldi.

1926 yılında Melkonian Eğitim Enstitüsü, şehrin kenarında kapılarını açtı. Soykırım yetimlerine bakmak amacıyla iki kardeş tarafından kurulan bu kurum, diasporanın dört bir yanından çocukların dillerini, müziklerini ve tarihlerini öğrenmek ve başkalarının yok etmeye çalıştığı bir kimliği yaşatmak için geldikleri, dünyanın en önemli Ermeni okullarından biri haline geldi.

Kuşaklar boyunca eski Lefkoşa'nın Ermeni mahallesi; kilisesinde, okulunda ve aile fırınlarında Batı Ermenicesiyle yankılandı. Adadaki diğer topluluklar gibi Ermeniler de 1974 olayları nedeniyle yerlerinden edildi ve bölündü, ancak yine de Kıbrıs'ın resmi olarak tanınan topluluklarından biri olarak ülkenin dokusuna işlenmeye devam ettiler.

Bu raptiye, bir hafıza ve direniş yerini işaret etmektedir. Neredeyse her şeyini kaybetmiş bir toplumun kendini yeniden inşa ettiği ve Ermeni dili ile ruhunun Lefkoşa'nın sokaklarında, kiliselerinde ve hikâyelerinde hâlâ varlığını sürdürdüğü yerdir.

story_translations.title: Δοκιμή: Ένα κοινό τραπέζι στην Κύπρο
story_translations.content: Αυτή είναι μια ενδεικτική δοκιmetική καταχώριση. Ένα κοινό γεύμα μπορεί να συνδέσει τους γείτονες μέσω του φαγητού, της γλώσσας και των αναμνήσεων. Η τοποθέτηση μιας ιστορίας στον τόπο της βοηθάει άλλους να ανακαλύψουν τις καθημερινές παραδόσεις που έχουν σημασία για μια κοινότητα.

story_translations.title: Demo: Kıbrıs'ta paylaşılan bir masa
story_translations.content: Bu, açıklayıcı nitelikte örnek bir girdidir. Birlikte paylaşılan bir öğün yemek, komşuları yemek, dil ve anılar aracılığıyla birbirine bağlayabilir. Bir hikayeyi ait olduğu yere sabitlemek, başkalarının bir topluluk için önem taşıyan günlük gelenekleri keşfetmesine yardımcı olur.

story_translations.title: Kaykay Günü 2026
story_translations.content: Dünya Kaykay Günü'nü bizimle kutlamak için geldiğiniz için hepinize teşekkür ederiz. Farklı şehirlerden, farklı gruplardan, farklı yaşlardan insanlar hepimiz aynı şey için bir araya geldi: kaykay. Başından sonuna kadar enerji inanılmazdı. Kaykaycılar, kameramanlar, fotoğrafçılar, arkadaşlar, dükkanlar, markalar ve yoldan geçenler güne ayrı bir değer kattı.

story_translations.title: Ημέρα Σκέιτ 2026
story_translations.content: Σας ευχαριστούμε όλους που ήρθατε να γιορτάσετε μαζί μας την Παγκόσμια Hμέρα Σκέιτ. Άνθρωποι έδωσαν το παρών από διαφορετικές πόλεις, διαφορετικές παρέες, διαφορετικές ηλικίες, όλοι για τον ίδιο λόγο: το σκέιτμπορντ. Η ενέργεια ήταν απίστευτη από την αρχή μέχρι το τέλος. Σκέιτερ, κάμεραμαν, φωτογράφοι, φίλοι, μαγαζιά, μάρκες και περαστικοί συνέβαλαν όλοι στη σημερινή ημέρα.
